title: Minimum Absolute Difference in BST
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair versus a single in-order traversal tracking the previous value.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary search tree, return the minimum absolute difference between the values of any two DIFFERENT nodes in the tree.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"BST\" plus \"minimum difference between any two values\"","In-order traversal of a BST produces sorted order; minimum difference in a sorted sequence is always between adjacent elements"],["No need to check every pair","A single in-order pass, tracking the previous value, suffices"]]}

blocks.text: Since in-order traversal of a BST visits node values in strictly increasing sorted order, the minimum difference between ANY two values in the tree must occur between two values that are ADJACENT in this sorted sequence, since any non-adjacent pair has a smaller-difference adjacent pair between them.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Closest Two Heights in a Lineup Sorted by Height
blocks.text: Picture people already lined up sorted by height, and wanting the two closest heights anywhere in the group. The closest pair must be standing right next to each other in this sorted line, never two people separated by others (since someone in between would be even closer to one of them).

blocks.caption: In-order traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order, so adjacent values in that order are the only candidates for the minimum difference

blocks.text: Result: 1. In-order gives 1,2,3,4,6; the closest adjacent pair (2,3) or (3,4) differs by 1.

Before comparing every pair of node values, notice that in-order traversal directly visits BST values in sorted order, so tracking just the PREVIOUS value visited and comparing it to the current one at each step captures every adjacent pair, which is all that is needed.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In-order traversal (left, node, right) of a BST visits nodes in strictly increasing value order.

Observation 2: The minimum difference in ANY sorted sequence is always between two adjacent elements, never a non-adjacent pair.

Observation 3: Performing in-order traversal while tracking the previously visited value lets each adjacent pair's difference be computed and compared to a running minimum in O(1) per node.

Observation 4: A single traversal therefore finds the true minimum difference across the whole tree.
This leads to a single in-order traversal, tracking the previous value and updating a running minimum difference at each step.
Collect all node values into a list, then check every pair for the minimum absolute difference.
Why the code is written this way

items: Checking every pair directly finds the minimum difference, guaranteed correct.
This costs O(n squared), unnecessary once the sorted in-order property is exploited.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared).
Space: O(n) for the values list.
Limitation: in-order traversal already visits values in sorted order, so tracking just the previous value achieves O(n) instead.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Since in-order traversal of a BST is already sorted, only adjacent pairs in this order can ever produce the minimum difference. Tracking the previous value during a single in-order pass, and updating a running minimum with each new comparison, replaces the need to check every pair explicitly.
Perform in-order traversal, tracking the previous visited value; at each node, update the minimum difference using (current value - previous value).

codes.python:
def get_minimum_difference(root):
    prev = None
    min_diff = float('inf')
    def inorder(node):
        nonlocal prev, min_diff
        if not node:
            return
        inorder(node.left)
        if prev is not None:
            min_diff = min(min_diff, node.val - prev)          # only adjacent pairs matter
        prev = node.val
        inorder(node.right)
    inorder(root)
    return min_diff

blocks.text: In-order traversal produces values in strictly increasing order, so the previous value at each step is always the immediately preceding value in sorted order. Comparing each new value only to this previous one covers every adjacent pair, and since the minimum difference must occur between adjacent values in a sorted sequence, this single pass finds the true minimum.

blocks.text: Checking every pair costs O(n squared); in-order traversal with a running previous value costs O(n), both using O(n) to O(height) space.

items: Pattern: in-order traversal of a BST is sorted, so only adjacent pairs matter for a minimum-difference query.
Core Idea: track the previous visited value during in-order traversal, updating a running minimum difference.
Time: O(n squared) for all-pairs, O(n) for in-order tracking.
Most Important Observation: BST in-order traversal is sorted, so the minimum difference is always between adjacent values.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible, foundational BST traversal problem.
